Guided trip

Across the Local Group

Our galaxy, its biggest companion, Andromeda, Triangulum. Then back to Earth.

Open the trip: Across the Local Group

Our galaxy, from outside

Nobody has seen the Milky Way from outside: this shape is a model built from measurements made inside it. It holds between one and four hundred billion stars, and the Sun is one of them, 27 000 light-years from the centre.

The Large Magellanic Cloud

This photograph of the Large Magellanic Cloud lines up with our sky. The biggest of our galaxy's companions and the fourth-largest galaxy in the group, it is a hundred and sixty thousand light-years away: pairs of its stars that eclipse each other tell us how far.

Andromeda, the other giant

Andromeda is two and a half million light-years away. With our Milky Way she is one of the group's two largest galaxies, and she is moving towards us. From our side this is a photograph; as we turn, a model takes over. Her tilt and rings are measured; the exact shape of her arms is ours.

Triangulum, the third spiral

This photograph from Chile lines up with our sky. The Triangulum Galaxy, third largest in the group, is about 2.7 million light-years away, a less certain distance than Andromeda's. On a very dark night some people can see it without a telescope.

The Local Group among its neighbours

Twenty-five million light-years out, the whole Local Group is the knot in the middle. Around it are eight hundred nearby galaxies from one catalogue. The brighter points have measured distances; the fainter grey-blue ones are only estimates.

Everything is drawn where it really is, from the HYG star database, OpenNGC and the planets’ own orbits (astronomy-engine).
